title: Leading space scientist reveals why extraterrestrial life has yet to be detected.
excerpt: According to researcher Vishal Gajjar, part of the reason why extraterrestrial life has yet to be detected stems from limitations in technology and research time.
content:
Considering the number of potentially habitable planets, the abundance of chemical elements that make up life, and the immense age of the universe, many researchers believe that the possibility of life existing elsewhere is entirely plausible. However, to date, humanity has yet to find conclusive evidence of extraterrestrial life .

Nevertheless, the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence (SETI) program continues to develop, attracting the attention of both the scientific community and the public.

In this field, the SETI Institute is one of the leading organizations, bringing together scientists from various disciplines to study the origins and potential existence of life in the universe.

One of the researchers directly involved in the search is Dr. Vishal Gajjar. His work focuses on detecting signals that could originate from the technology of extraterrestrial civilizations, through observations across the Milky Way galaxy.

How can technological signals reveal the presence of extraterrestrial beings?

According to Dr. Vishal Gajjar, his research goal is to find technological signatures, also known as technosignatures.

These are traces that could indicate the presence of a life form that has developed advanced technology.

He stated that the search for technological signs is not separate from the search for biological life, but can be seen as an extension of this research activity.

While the search for life could simply begin in locations near Earth within the Solar System, the search for more advanced civilizations allows scientists to explore a much larger region of space.

One notable characteristic is that the signal has an extremely narrow frequency range, similar to a single tone with a defined frequency.

To date, scientists are unaware of any common natural processes that could produce such a unique type of signal.

If a signal is detected that meets these characteristics, researchers may consider the possibility that it was created by a technologically advanced civilization.

However, this is not enough evidence to confirm that the signals are from extraterrestrial beings.

Scientists still need to check for and rule out natural sources of interference or man-made interference.

In addition to narrow-frequency signals, other types of signals are also of interest, such as radio signals emitted in regular rhythms or patterns.

If they have the right structure, they can be traces of a method of information transmission.

The major challenge lies in the fact that humans still cannot fully comprehend the technologies that an extraterrestrial civilization might utilize.

If that civilization had advanced far beyond humanity, their methods of communication might have been entirely different, perhaps even based on technologies unknown to current science.

However, if they use radio waves, scientists can still search for signals with a clear structure and the ability to distinguish them from background noise.

To search for signs of technology, researchers use radio telescopes to observe various sources of radiation in the sky.

They surveyed many stars and regions within the Milky Way, searching for radio signals with unusual characteristics.

The SETI Institute also operates its own telescope system in California, USA, called the Allen Telescope Array.

This system consists of 42 antennas, each with a diameter of approximately 6.1m, arranged over an area of ​​about 300m.

That configuration allows scientists to observe multiple targets and collect data to aid in the search for signals of unknown origin.

However, data collection is only the first step. The volume of information from radio astronomical observations is enormous, while the signal we are looking for may be weak, fleeting, or obscured by noise.

Therefore, the ability to process data and detect less common patterns is crucial to the success of the SETI program.

The building blocks of life are found throughout the universe.

Why is Gajjar optimistic about the possibility of extraterrestrial life? One reason is that scientists are increasingly finding more basic chemical components related to life in the universe.

He said that recent studies show that the building blocks of life are not unique to Earth.

For example, samples collected from the asteroid Bennu have been found to contain numerous amino acids and important organic compounds.

Some of these compounds are related to the chemistry of life, although this does not mean that complete DNA or living organisms have been found on the asteroid.

Such a discovery reinforces the notion that the building blocks necessary for life can form and exist in a variety of environments outside of Earth.

Gajjar argues that if these basic components are common throughout the universe, and there are countless Earth-like planets located in regions with suitable temperatures around stars, then the emergence of life elsewhere is a promising possibility.

However, one fundamental question remains unanswered: did life on Earth originate here, or were its components, or even its earliest forms, brought here from elsewhere?

Scientists currently lack sufficient evidence to draw definitive conclusions about the ultimate origin of life.

It can be said that the universe has many potential environments and materials for complex chemical processes to take place.

If suitable conditions existed in many places, the possibility that Earth was the first and only place to have life would hardly be considered a given.

Why hasn't humanity discovered extraterrestrial life yet?

Although the possibility of extraterrestrial life is considered interesting by many scientists, humanity still lacks conclusive evidence. According to Gajjar, this is partly due to limitations in technology and research time.

On a cosmic scale, humanity has only begun systematically searching for extraterrestrial life in the last 60 years or so.

This period of time is but a blink of an eye compared to the billions of years of the universe's history.

Scientists don't yet know exactly what kind of signals to look for.

Current methods primarily focus on signal types that humans are capable of visualizing and detecting using the technology available.

This means that a signal that actually exists may still be outside the current search range.

The situation is gradually changing thanks to more powerful computer processors and advanced data analysis tools. These technologies allow researchers to sift through massive amounts of data, detecting patterns that are difficult to discern using traditional methods.

Gajjar argues that the universe's silence so far doesn't prove that there's no life out there. It only shows that humanity's ability to detect life may be lower than initially expected.

In his view, the so-called "great silence" should be seen as a limitation in humanity's search strategy, rather than a fundamental law that the entire universe is silent.

(According to SciTechDaily, Earthsky, Skyatnightmagazine)
